item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports using item text in sequential recommendation, but does not establish the exact proposed combination: a scratch-trained title/description encoder jointly optimized with NextItNet and semantic hard negatives. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) combines textual item representations with sequential modeling and reports improvements on Amazon datasets. However, it uses BERT, self-attention and reviews; its strongest reported text contribution comes from reviews. Its results therefore offer motivation, not direct evidence for the permitted title/description-only, scratch-trained setting. [NextItNet’s original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) establishes residual dilated causal convolutions as the sequential backbone.\n\nHard-negative research suggests balancing informativeness against false negatives. [ESANS (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16077) explores semantic-aware negative sampling for retrieval, while [Enhanced Bayesian Personalized Ranking (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) explicitly addresses misleading false negatives during hard-negative mining. Neither validates this exact NextItNet configuration. A task-compatible hypothesis is a small, randomly initialized token encoder pooling titles/descriptions into a gated residual addition to item-ID embeddings, jointly trained inside one causal-convolution model. Mix random negatives with a limited fraction of text-similar candidates, exclude observed training positives, and introduce harder candidates gradually. These are experimental design inferences, requiring validation against the corrected ID-only baseline; text similarity alone does not establish user dislike or item compatibility."}
